parts.title: What happens to young people who have MGUS, a harmless-looking blood protein that can turn into cancer?
parts.abstract:
Abstract

MGUS (monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance) is a condition in which the blood contains a small amount of an unusual protein, called the M protein, made by a single type of white blood cell. It is rare in young people: fewer than 0.3% of people under 40 have it, and they make up about 2% of everyone with MGUS. We suspected that MGUS found in young people might be more likely to turn into a cancer.

We studied 249 people who had MGUS before they turned 40. At the time their MGUS was found, 135 of them also had an immune-related illness. These were infections, autoimmune diseases (where the immune system attacks the body's own tissues) or other inflammatory diseases.

Over 5 years, 6.0% of these young patients had developed multiple myeloma or a related disorder. Over 10 years, the figure was 13.8%. The amount of M protein in the blood was a statistically significant risk factor for this change. A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no link, a pattern this strong would rarely appear by chance alone. For M protein, the hazard ratio was 4.2, with a 95% confidence interval of 2.2 to 7.9. A hazard ratio compares how quickly something happens in one group with how quickly it happens in another. The confidence interval is the range of values that fit our data well.

Patients without an immune-related illness tended to have a higher risk of change, with a hazard ratio of 2.36 (95% confidence interval 0.85 to 6.52, p = 0.088). This result was not statistically significant, so our study could not show a real difference between the two groups.

The M protein disappeared in 36 patients (14% of the 249). It was more likely to disappear in patients who had an immune-related illness. The relative risk was 1.9 (95% confidence interval 1.02 to 3.6), meaning the M protein disappeared 1.9 times as often in that group.

Young people with MGUS have about the same risk of change as older people: 1.4% per year. More than half of them are found to have MGUS while they are being treated for an immune-related illness. Patients with an immune-related illness may have a lower risk of change.

Subject terms: Lymphoproliferative disorders (cancers of the immune system's white blood cells), Risk factors, Myeloma, VDJ recombination (the way immune cells build their antibodies), Myeloma
parts.introduction_first:
MGUS (monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance) is a condition in which the blood contains a small amount of an unusual protein, called the M protein, made by a single type of white blood cell. To count as MGUS, three things must be true. First, the M protein in the blood is 3 grams per decilitre or less. Second, fewer than 10% of the cells in the bone marrow are plasma cells, the white blood cells that make antibodies. Third, the M protein or these cells have not damaged any organ. Doctors also check for the "CRAB" signs of cancer: high calcium in the blood, kidney damage, bone damage and a low number of red blood cells.

In people over 50, MGUS is seen as a warning sign that may lead to multiple myeloma or to related cancers of the immune system. In these older patients, about 1% of people with MGUS develop a cancer each year. MGUS is very rare in young people under 40: fewer than 0.3% of them have it, and they make up about 2% of everyone with MGUS. We still know very little about how MGUS develops and changes over time in young people.
parts.conclusion:
Conclusions

Young people with MGUS have about the same risk of change as older people: 1.4% per year. About half of them are found to have MGUS while they are being treated for an immune-related illness. In these patients, the M protein is smaller and more likely to disappear. It may also be less likely to turn into cancer than in patients whose MGUS is found without any immune-related illness at the same time. Our study adds to what we know about MGUS and similar blood protein conditions, and about what causes them.
parts.introduction_rest:
Many different risk factors have been linked to the chance that MGUS will turn into another plasma cell disorder, a cancer of the white blood cells that make antibodies. However, nobody has looked closely at how these risk factors matter in young people who have MGUS. In particular, no one has studied how immune-related illnesses affect the course of MGUS. These include autoimmune diseases, infections and other inflammatory diseases that happen at the same time as a blood protein condition like MGUS.

Earlier studies give some clues. Lindqvist and colleagues carried out a large case–control study, which compares people who have a condition with people who do not. They found that the risk of having MGUS was higher in people with every kind of immune-related illness. Brown and colleagues found a similar link for multiple myeloma: people with immune-related illnesses were 15–29% more likely to develop it. Autoimmune diseases have also been linked to a higher risk of both MGUS and multiple myeloma. In people with autoimmune diseases, multiple myeloma tends to start at a younger age.

One idea may help explain these links. In immune-related illnesses, the immune system is constantly being set off. This can make B cells, the white blood cells that make antibodies, work poorly. Scientists have suggested that this could be a risk factor for cancers that start from a single type of plasma cell.

We designed this study to learn more about how MGUS develops and changes over time in young people. In particular, we wanted to find out whether MGUS in young people follows a more aggressive course, meaning it is more likely to turn into multiple myeloma or a related disorder. We looked at how MGUS turns out in a large number of young patients, and especially at how having an immune-related illness at the same time affects whether MGUS changes.
parts.methods:
Patients and methods

We used a database kept at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, which records patients with blood protein conditions as they are seen over time. From it, we picked out 249 patients who were younger than 40 when their MGUS was found, and who had been checked between January 1, 1997 and December 31, 2016. Every patient met the rules for MGUS. Their M protein in the blood was 3 grams per decilitre or less. If their bone marrow had been checked, 10% or fewer of the cells in it were plasma cells.

We left some patients out. We did not include patients whose MGUS came with damage to the nerves in the arms and legs, and who were later diagnosed with POEMS syndrome, a different condition that can cause nerve damage. We also left out patients who had had a cancer of the immune system's white blood cells before, and who had been given chemotherapy or steroids for more than 4 weeks before their MGUS was found. Some patients had two different M proteins at once, which doctors call biclonal gammopathy. For these, we used the larger of the two. Some patients had light-chain MGUS, where the M protein is made only of the small "light chain" part of an antibody. We did not include these patients in any analysis that used the size of the M protein. The Mayo Clinic Institutional Review Board, which checks that research is safe and fair, approved the study. We followed the Declaration of Helsinki, a set of ethical rules for research with people, and the 1996 guidelines of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a US law that protects patients' medical information.

For every patient, we recorded their age and sex. We also recorded the main symptoms they had reported most recently before their MGUS was found, and whether any family member had a plasma cell disorder or a cancer of the blood. We recorded the type of M protein and its size from the day the MGUS was found. We also used four other blood and bone marrow results, if they had been done at least 3 months before the disease changed. These were beta2 microglobulin (a protein that can rise when the body is under stress or when there are many plasma cells), lactate dehydrogenase (an enzyme that can rise when cells are damaged), the ratio of free light chains in the blood, and the percentage of plasma cells in the bone marrow, if this had been measured.

Sometimes the M protein was found only by immunofixation, a test that identifies the type of protein, but was too small to measure on electrophoresis, a test that sorts proteins by size. In those cases, we recorded the size of the M protein as 0.001 grams per decilitre. We collected information on immune-related illnesses from patients' hospital and clinic records. These included autoimmune diseases, inflammatory diseases and infections. We then split the patients into two groups: those who had any immune-related illness at the time their MGUS was found, and those who did not.

We counted a patient as having changed from MGUS when they developed one of several conditions. These were smoldering multiple myeloma (SMM), multiple myeloma (MM), macroglobulinemia (a build-up of a large type of antibody protein), non-Hodgkin lymphoma, immunoglobulin (heavy) light chain amyloidosis (a build-up of protein fragments in the body's tissues) or chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

We counted a patient as having SMM when their symptoms made us suspect the disease was changing and called for further tests, such as a bone marrow biopsy (a small sample taken from the bone marrow). However, these worrying symptoms did not come from the events that define multiple myeloma, and the blood and bone marrow results did not meet the rules for diagnosing active multiple myeloma. We diagnosed SMM when, during follow-up, the M protein was above 3 grams per decilitre and/or 10–59% of the cells in the bone marrow were clonal plasma cells (plasma cells that all come from the same abnormal cell), and there were no events that define multiple myeloma.

Most patients (67%) did not have a bone marrow biopsy when their MGUS was found, which matches how we work in our clinic. None of the patients in this study were treated while they had SMM. No one in this group went on to develop active multiple myeloma. We recorded whether the M protein disappeared, and when, when immunofixation tests were negative on two checks in a row, at least 6 months apart, during follow-up.

To compare the two groups, we used two statistical tests. The chi-square test checks whether the share of patients with a certain feature differs between groups. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test checks whether one group's values tend to be higher or lower than another's. We used them to see whether the basic features of patients with immune-related illnesses differed from those of patients without them.

We also looked at two kinds of survival. Progression-free survival is the time from the MGUS diagnosis until the disease changes. Overall survival is the time until a patient dies. We measured both for all patients together and for each of the two groups, using the Kaplan–Meier method. This method follows how many patients are still free of change, or still alive, as time goes on. We compared the groups with the Wilcoxon test and the log-rank test, which checks whether the survival curves of two groups differ.

Next, we used a Cox model, a method that estimates how much each factor is linked to the risk of change over time. First, we looked at each factor on its own: age, the size of the M protein, the type of immunoglobulin (the main part of the antibody), the type of light chain, and whether the patient had an immune-related illness. Then we used a Cox model that looked at several factors together, to see how age, the size of the M protein and the presence of an immune-related illness each affected progression-free survival on their own. We repeated all of these analyses for overall survival, and also for the patients whose M protein disappeared, leaving them out of the analysis.

For every test, we called a result statistically significant when its p value was below 0.05. This means that if there were really no difference, a gap this large would appear by chance alone less than 5% of the time. We used the program JMP® Pro 14.0 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA) for the statistics.
parts.results:
Results

We found 249 patients who had MGUS before they turned 40 and who met the rules for taking part in our study. Table 1 shows who they were and what their blood tests showed when their MGUS was first found. Their median age was 35 years, and 130 of them (52%) were women. Most patients (179, or 72%) were found to have MGUS between the ages of 30 and 39. At the same time as their MGUS, 135 patients (54%) had an immune-related illness. Table 2 lists these illnesses.

A family history of blood cancer was present in 14 patients (6%). Six of these (2%) had a family history of plasma cell disorders, which are cancers of the cells that make antibodies. Table 3 shows the main complaints that led doctors to find MGUS, grouped by the part of the body they came from.

The M protein in our patients was fairly small compared with what other researchers have reported. Its median amount was 0.27 grams per decilitre, and the middle half of patients had between 0.001 and 0.43 grams per decilitre. In 172 patients (69%), the M protein was so small that we could not measure its amount. We could only detect it with immunofixation, a lab test that sorts the proteins in the blood by type. The median time we followed these 172 patients was 2.9 years. Only 11 patients (4%) had more than 1.5 grams of M protein per decilitre in their blood.

The M protein is a type of antibody, and antibodies come in different types, called IgG, IgA and IgM. Of all patients, 69% had IgG, 10% IgA, 15% IgM and 5% something else. The 5% were 12 patients with biclonal gammopathy, meaning two different M proteins, and 1 patient with light chain MGUS, meaning the M protein was made of only the light part of an antibody.

An antibody is built from a heavy part and a light part, and the light part comes in two types, kappa and lambda. Leaving out the biclonal patients, 59% of patients had kappa and 41% had lambda.

Some patients had a serum free light chain test before their MGUS changed. This test measures the light parts of antibodies floating freely in the blood, and compares the two types. Of all patients, 69 (28%) had this test. Among patients without an immune-related illness, 33 (29%) had it, and among those with one, 36 (27%) had it. The test was abnormal in 8 patients without an immune-related illness (24%) and in 4 patients with one (11%). This difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.20).

We looked at the bone marrow, the soft tissue inside bones where blood cells are made, in 82 patients (33%). The median share of plasma cells in the bone marrow was 2%, with the middle half of patients between 2% and 5%.

Patients without an immune-related illness tended to have more M protein than patients with one (p = 0.057). Over the 2.9 years we followed them, the M protein disappeared in 36 patients. The median time until it disappeared was 1.5 years, and it took anywhere from 0.2 to 8.6 years. In these 36 patients, the M protein had been too small to measure at the start.

The M protein was more likely to disappear in patients with an immune-related illness than in patients without one. The relative risk was 1.91, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.02 to 3.59 (p = 0.03). This means the M protein disappeared 1.91 times as often in the group with an immune-related illness. Of the 36 patients whose M protein first disappeared, two had it come back again: one 6 years later and one 9 years later.

In total, 16 young patients (6%) developed a change in their MGUS (Table 4). Nine developed smoldering multiple myeloma, a form of multiple myeloma that is still not causing damage. Four had active multiple myeloma, one had Waldenström macroglobulinemia, and two had non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Thirty-six patients died, and three of them died of myeloma.

By 5 years, 6.0% of all patients had developed smoldering multiple myeloma, multiple myeloma or a related disorder. By 10 years, the figure was 13.8% (Fig. 1).

To look for risk factors, we used a Cox analysis. This method looks at how quickly something happens over time, and it can look at one factor at a time (a univariate analysis) or several factors together. When we looked at one factor at a time, the amount of M protein was a statistically significant risk factor for change. The hazard ratio was 4.23, with a 95% confidence interval of 2.17 to 7.91 (p < 0.0001). We then took into account whether patients had an immune-related illness. Even then, the amount of M protein stayed a strong risk factor for change (hazard ratio 3.90, 95% confidence interval 2.0 to 7.34; p = 0.0002). Age, the type of antibody, the type of light chain and having an immune-related illness did not have a statistically significant effect on how the disease turned out.

We saw similar results when we left out the 36 patients whose M protein had disappeared. For all patients, the risk of change by 5 years was 7.6% and by 10 years was 17.7%. For patients with an immune-related illness, it was 2.2% and 14.1%. For patients without one, it was 14.0% and 21.8%. The log-rank test gave p = 0.084 and the Wilcoxon test gave p = 0.032 (hazard ratio 2.49, 95% confidence interval 0.85 to 7.30).
parts.discussion:
Discussion

We studied what happens to 249 people who had MGUS before they turned 40. On average, 1.4% of these young patients developed a cancer each year. That is similar to the rate in older patients. MGUS is uncommon in young people, but finding it early did not mean the disease would be more aggressive or more slow-moving.

The amount of M protein in the blood predicted whether young patients would go on to develop a plasma cell disorder (a cancer of the antibody-making cells) or a lymphoid disorder (a cancer of other white blood cells). This is a strong risk factor: for every extra unit of M protein, the risk of change was 3 times higher. Earlier studies of MGUS, including in older patients, also found that the amount of M protein was a strong risk factor for change. Our study shows the same thing in young patients.

We did not find a statistically significant difference in the risk of change between patients with an immune-related illness and patients without one. There was a trend towards a higher risk in patients without an immune-related illness. The hazard ratio was 2.36, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.85 to 6.52 and p = 0.088. In the early part of the follow-up, patients without an immune-related illness changed more often than patients with one. Over the whole long follow-up, this difference disappeared.

One possible explanation is lead-time bias. This happens when a disease is found earlier, so the time from diagnosis to cancer looks longer even though the cancer would have happened at the same time. In our study, patients with an immune-related illness were probably diagnosed with MGUS earlier in its course than patients without one. Their MGUS was found during tests done as part of their care for the autoimmune illness.

It is possible that young patients with MGUS and no immune-related illness had already started on the path to a plasma cell disorder in the past. In the early part of our follow-up, these patients changed more often into plasma cell disorders because their MGUS had been present for longer. Patients with an immune-related illness had a shorter history of MGUS. Over the long follow-up, the two groups did not differ in how long they stayed free of change.

The M protein in our study was fairly small compared with earlier studies. There are two possible reasons. First, our young patients were probably diagnosed at an earlier stage of their disease. Older patients often live with MGUS for a long time without knowing it, and it is found only by accident. In most patients, the amount of M protein slowly rises over the course of the disease. An immune-related illness may be an early trigger for plasma cell disorders. This fits with reports that, in patients with immune-related illnesses, the M protein is often too small to measure.

Second, the M protein that is too small to measure in patients with immune-related illnesses might not be true MGUS, because some of it did not last. In 36 patients, we saw the M protein disappear. In a smaller number of patients, we could not tell what happened to the M protein, because we lost contact with them after they were diagnosed with MGUS. We found that the M protein was more likely to disappear in patients with an immune-related illness than in patients without one. Patients with an immune-related illness also had less M protein in their blood.

We do not know why the M protein disappears. Murray and colleagues reported that M proteins too small to measure were less likely to last: 30% of them disappeared in their study. They also found that, among patients whose M protein did not last, 55% had an immune disease or were taking medicine that changes the immune system. A few studies of small groups of patients found something similar: the M protein was small and short-lived during sudden kidney failure and during various infections.

The idea that patients without an immune-related illness may change more often would fit with the hypothesis that an M protein too small to measure is not true MGUS that can turn into cancer. Medicines that calm the immune system could also stop the M protein from lasting. These include steroids, which may lower the amount of M protein in the blood, and cyclophosphamide, a drug that works against myeloma.

It is worth studying what happens in the long run when the M protein comes and goes. Even after the M protein disappears, it could come back. Of the 36 patients whose M protein disappeared, two had it return: one after 6 years and the other after 9 years from when it first disappeared. In both patients, the M protein that came back was the same type as the first one. Both had been taking medicines to calm their immune system for a long time for their underlying diseases, and the return of the M protein was not linked to stopping these medicines. This finding goes against the idea that a short-lived M protein is harmless. Longer follow-up is needed to understand this better.

Our study has limitations. We could not study how the free light chain ratio in the blood affects the future of young patients with MGUS, because too few patients had this test done. This ratio compares two small parts of the antibody, called light chains, that float freely in the blood. It may play a major role in the future of the disease, as it does in older people, but this needs more study. We also do not know exactly how much steroids helped the M protein disappear, because we did not have the percentage of patients who were taking steroids. Steroids are known to be one of the treatments for myeloma and can lower the M protein.

The follow-up in our study was short. Many of these patients came to Mayo Clinic for complex diseases and were found to have MGUS by accident when they were young. They stopped coming back after a few visits to Mayo Clinic. Perhaps their general doctor was following their MGUS. Smouldering multiple myeloma (SMM) is a stage before cancer in which the blood has more plasma cells than in MGUS but no organ damage. It can last a very long time without symptoms and does not need treatment. Future studies would be more useful to doctors if they recorded whether patients needed chemotherapy after they developed smouldering multiple myeloma.
